paragraphs: But if the sexes really are to live in a state of warfare, if nature has marked it out for them, let men at least act nobly, or let pride whisper to them that the victory is base when all they overcome is sensibility. The real conquest is over affection that has not been taken by surprise — as when a woman, like Heloisa, deliberately gives up the whole world for love. I am not now weighing the wisdom or virtue of such a sacrifice; I only maintain that it was a sacrifice to affection, and not merely to sensibility, though she had her share of sensibility. And I must be allowed to call her a modest woman, before I leave this part of the subject with the remark that until men are more chaste, women will be immodest. Where, indeed, could modest women find husbands from whom they would not constantly turn away in disgust? Modesty must be cultivated equally by both sexes, or it will always remain a sickly hothouse plant, while the affectation of it — the fig leaf borrowed by wantonness — may add relish to voluptuous enjoyments.

Men will probably still insist that woman ought to have more modesty than man; but it is not dispassionate reasoners who will most eagerly oppose my opinion. No, it will be the men of fancy, the favourites of the sex, who outwardly respect and inwardly despise the weak creatures they toy with in this way. They cannot bring themselves to give up the highest sensual gratification, or even to acquire a taste for the refined pleasure of virtue — self-denial.
To look at the subject from another angle, I will confine my remarks to women.

The absurd falsehoods told to children out of mistaken notions of modesty tend very early to inflame their imaginations and set their little minds working on subjects that nature never meant them to think about until the body had reached some degree of maturity. At that stage the passions naturally begin to take over from the senses as the instruments that unfold the understanding and form the moral character.

It is in nurseries and boarding schools, I fear, that girls are first spoiled, and particularly in the latter. A number of girls sleep in the same room and wash together. Now, though I would be sorry to taint an innocent creature’s mind by instilling false delicacy, or those indecent prudish notions that early warnings about the other sex naturally breed, I would be very anxious to prevent their acquiring indelicate or immodest habits; and since many girls have learned very indelicate tricks from ignorant servants, mixing them together in this indiscriminate way is highly improper.

To tell the truth, women are in general too familiar with one another, and this leads to the gross degree of familiarity that so often makes married life unhappy. Why, in the name of decency, should sisters, close female friends, or ladies and their maids be so grossly familiar as to forget the respect that one human creature owes another? That squeamish delicacy which shrinks from the most disgusting tasks when affection or humanity leads us to watch at a sickbed is contemptible. But why women in good health should be more familiar with one another than men are, when they boast of their superior delicacy, is an inconsistency in manners that I have never been able to explain.

To preserve health and beauty, I would earnestly recommend frequent ablutions — to give my advice a dignified word so that it does not offend the fastidious ear. Girls ought to be taught, by example, to wash and dress alone, whatever their rank; and if habit should make them need a little help, let them not ask for it until that part of the business is over which ought never to be done in front of a fellow creature, because it is an insult to the majesty of human nature. I say this not on grounds of modesty but of decency; for the care some modest women take not to let their legs be seen, while making a display of that very care, is as childish as it is immodest.*

(*Footnote. I remember coming across a sentence in a book on education that made me smile. “It would be needless to caution you against putting your hand, by chance, under your neck-handkerchief; for a modest woman never did so!”)

I could go further still, and comment on some even more indelicate customs into which men never fall. Secrets are told where silence ought to reign; and that regard for cleanliness which some religious sects have perhaps carried too far — especially the Essenes among the Jews, who made an insult to God of what is only an insult to humanity — is violated in a brutal manner. How can DELICATE women force on others’ notice that part of our animal functions which is so very disgusting? And is it not quite rational to conclude that women who have not been taught to respect the human nature of their own sex in these particulars will not long respect the mere difference of sex in their husbands? Once their maidenly bashfulness is lost, I have in fact generally observed that women fall back into their old habits and treat their husbands as they treated their sisters or female acquaintances.

Besides, because their minds are not cultivated, women are very often driven by necessity to what I call, in plain terms, bodily wit; and their intimacies are of the same kind. In short, in both mind and body they are too intimate. The decent personal reserve that is the foundation of dignity of character must be kept up between women, or their minds will never gain strength or modesty.

For this reason, too, I object to shutting up many females together in nurseries, schools or convents. I cannot remember without indignation the jokes and tomboyish pranks that groups of young women indulged in when, in my youth, chance threw me, an awkward country girl, into their company. They were almost on a level with the double meanings that shake the dinner table when the wine has gone round freely. But it is useless to try to keep the heart pure unless the head is stocked with ideas and set to work comparing them, so as to acquire judgment by generalizing simple ideas, and modesty by letting the understanding dampen the sensibility.

It may be thought that I lay too much stress on personal reserve; but it is always the handmaid of modesty. So much so that if I were to name the graces that ought to adorn beauty, I would at once exclaim: cleanliness, neatness and personal reserve. It is obvious, I suppose, that the reserve I mean has nothing sexual in it, and that I think it EQUALLY necessary in both sexes. Indeed, that reserve and cleanliness which lazy women too often neglect are so necessary that I will venture to affirm this: when two or three women live in the same house, the one who pays this kind of habitual respect to her own person will be the most respected by the men of the family who live with them, leaving love entirely out of the question.

When members of a household meet in the morning, an affectionate seriousness will naturally prevail, especially if each is looking forward to carrying out the day’s duties. It may be thought fanciful, but this feeling has often risen spontaneously in my mind. After breathing the sweet, bracing morning air, I have been pleased to see the same kind of freshness in the faces I particularly loved; I was glad to see them braced, as it were, for the day, and ready to run their course with the sun. In this way the greetings of affection in the morning are more respectful than the familiar tenderness that often draws out the evening’s talk. Indeed, I have often felt hurt, not to say disgusted, when a friend whom I had left fully dressed the evening before appeared with her clothes thrown on anyhow, because she chose to indulge herself in bed until the last moment.

Domestic affection can be kept alive only by these neglected attentions. Yet if men and women took half as much trouble to be habitually neat in their dress as they take to ornament, or rather to disfigure, their persons, much would be done towards achieving purity of mind. But women dress only to gratify men of gallantry; for the lover is always best pleased with simple clothing that fits close to the figure. There is an impertinence in ornaments that repels affection, because love always clings to the idea of home.

As a sex, women are habitually indolent, and everything tends to make them so. I do not forget the bursts of activity that sensibility produces; but since these flights of feeling only make the evil worse, they are not to be confused with the slow, orderly walk of reason. In reality, their mental and bodily indolence is so great that until their bodies are strengthened and their understandings enlarged by active exertion, there is little reason to expect modesty to take the place of bashfulness. They may find it prudent to put on its appearance; but that fair veil will be worn only on holidays.

Perhaps there is no virtue that blends so kindly with every other as modesty does. It is the pale moonbeam that makes every virtue it softens more appealing, lending a mild grandeur to the narrowed horizon. Nothing can be more beautiful than the poetic fiction that makes Diana, with her silver crescent, the goddess of chastity. I have sometimes thought that a modest lady of antiquity, wandering with measured step in some lonely retreat, must have felt a glow of conscious dignity when, after gazing on the soft, shadowy landscape, she calmly and fervently invited the gentle reflection of her sister’s beams to turn to her chaste bosom.

A Christian has still nobler motives to urge her to preserve her chastity and acquire modesty, for her body has been called the Temple of the living God — of that God who requires more than a modest demeanour. His eye searches the heart. Let her remember, then, that if she hopes to find favour in the sight of purity itself, her chastity must be founded on modesty and not on worldly prudence; otherwise, truly, a good reputation will be her only reward. For that solemn intercourse, that sacred communion, which virtue establishes between man and his Maker must give rise to the wish to be pure as he is pure!

After the foregoing remarks it is almost superfluous to add that I consider immodest all those feminine airs of maturity which follow bashfulness and to which truth is sacrificed in order to secure a husband’s heart — or rather to force him to remain a lover when nature, had her workings not been interrupted, would have made love give way to friendship. The tenderness a man feels for the mother of his children is an excellent substitute for the ardour of unsatisfied passion; but for women to feign an unnatural coldness of constitution in order to prolong that ardour is indelicate, not to say immodest. Women as well as men ought to have the common appetites and passions of their nature; these are brutal only when reason does not check them. But the obligation to check them is the duty of mankind, not a sexual duty. In these respects nature may safely be left to herself; let women only acquire knowledge and humanity, and love will teach them modesty. There is no need for falsehoods, as disgusting as they are futile; for studied rules of behaviour deceive only shallow observers, and a man of sense soon sees through the affectation and despises it.

How young people behave towards each other as men and women is the last thing that should be thought of in education. In fact, behaviour in most circumstances is now given so much thought that simplicity of character is rarely seen. Yet if men were anxious only to cultivate each virtue and let it take firm root in the mind, the grace that results from it — its natural outward mark — would soon strip affectation of its showy plumes; for conduct not founded on truth is as deceptive as it is unstable!

(Footnote. I have often been disgusted by the way many newly married women behave. They seem anxious that their husbands should never forget the privilege of marriage, and they appear to take no pleasure in his company unless he is acting the lover. Love’s reign must indeed be short when its flame is perpetually fanned like this without ever being fed any solid fuel.)

If you really wish to possess modesty, my sisters, you must remember that possessing virtue of any kind is incompatible with ignorance and vanity! You must acquire that sobriety of mind which only the performance of duties and the pursuit of knowledge can inspire, or you will still remain in a doubtful, dependent situation, and be loved only while you are beautiful! The downcast eye, the rosy blush, the retiring grace are all proper in their season; but modesty, being the child of reason, cannot long survive alongside a sensibility that reflection has not tempered. Besides, when love, even innocent love, is the whole business of your lives, your hearts will be too soft to give modesty that quiet retreat where she delights to live, in close union with humanity.
